strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated new direction for generative classifiers by leveraging VAR's tractable likelihood, addressing the main scalability bottleneck of diffusion-based generative classifiers; the reported 160x speed-up with less than 1% accuracy drop relative to the diffusion classifier is a concrete and significant practical improvement.

The comparative analysis is well-controlled: all generative models are trained on the same data (ImageNet), so observed property differences are attributable to the model family/objective rather than training data, and the paper honestly reports a negative result — the robustness properties of diffusion classifiers do not transfer to VAR — which is scientifically valuable.

The techniques (likelihood smoothing to mitigate VQ-token sensitivity, partial-scale candidate pruning exploiting VAR's coarse-to-fine structure, and CCA finetuning) are sensibly designed, each motivated by clear empirical observations, and ablations (Table 2, Table 4) isolate their individual contributions, including an interesting analysis of the generative/discriminative trade-off across model sizes.

The token-wise PMI explainability and the class-incremental learning experiment are natural but genuinely useful demonstrations enabled by the tractable likelihood, and the failure case analysis in the appendix adds credibility.
Reproducibility is well handled: pseudo-code, detailed evaluation subset construction (WordNet ID lists, sampling procedures), and public baselines are provided.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core ideas (smoothed likelihoods, two-/multi-stage candidate pruning, borrowed CCA finetuning objective) are individually incremental engineering contributions rather than fundamentally new methodology; token-wise PMI explainability is a fairly direct consequence of autoregressive likelihood factorization.

The evaluation scale is limited: results are on a 100-class ImageNet subset rather than full ImageNet-1k, and distribution-shift evaluations use only 10 samples per class (about 1,000 images per dataset), which introduces high variance and weakens claims about robustness differences between methods; no confidence intervals or seeds are reported.

The proposed method still trails discriminative classifiers on nearly all distribution-shift benchmarks (e.g., 79.3 vs 86.9 on ImageNet-V2, 33.1 vs 52.5 on ImageNet-R), and CCA finetuning reduces robustness on ImageNet-A and ImageNet-Sketch, so the practical benefit case rests mainly on the in-distribution accuracy-efficiency trade-off; the significance for practitioners choosing classifiers is thus narrow.

The class-incremental learning result is only a small proof-of-concept (10 classes, 2 tasks) with a from-scratch VAR-d8; the costs of training an independent generative model per task compared to rehearsal or regularization baselines beyond CWR are not analyzed, so claims of 'inherent resistance' to forgetting are under-supported at scale.

Likelihood smoothing resembles randomized-smoothing style Monte Carlo averaging, and its connection to prior robustness/smoothing literature is not discussed; the choice of sigma=0.1 and S=10 appears tuned empirically without sensitivity analysis in the main text.

Runtime comparisons are partially estimated (diffusion classifier runtime on a single A6000 while actual computations used heterogeneous hardware), which makes the headline 160x speed-up somewhat approximate.

strengths: The idea of using VAR's tractable likelihood for generative classification is a reasonable and timely extension beyond diffusion-based generative classifiers, and the paper is clearly written and well-organized.

The comparative analysis is refreshingly honest: the authors openly report that the robustness properties of diffusion-based classifiers do not transfer to VAR, which adds scientific value and clarifies that the denoising objective, not generativity per se, drives those properties.

The analysis in Appendix C on the generative-discriminative trade-off across model sizes (Table 4, Fig. 4) — showing that larger models dilute class-conditional information — is an interesting empirical observation with useful implications.

The accuracy-efficiency trade-off is well documented: a 160× speed-up over the diffusion classifier with <1% accuracy drop on ImageNet-100 is a concrete, measurable improvement, and the ablation (Table 2) cleanly separates the contributions of likelihood smoothing and CCA finetuning.
The reproducibility statement is above average: pseudo-code, exact class lists (WordNet IDs), subsampling procedures, and pointers to all pretrained models are provided.
weaknesses: The paper's central motivation is scalability of generative classifiers to large class counts, yet all evaluation is on ImageNet-100 (100 classes). The scalability claim is never actually demonstrated on ImageNet-1k, which is the setting where the efficiency argument matters most. The headline result is therefore weaker than the framing suggests.

The proposed method does not outperform any strong baseline on accuracy: A-VARC+ (89.32) trails ViT-B/16 (94.20) and even the diffusion classifier DC(25,250) (90.30) on ImageNet-100, and underperforms discriminative models on nearly all distribution-shift datasets. The contribution reduces to an efficiency improvement within an approach that is still strictly worse than standard discriminative classifiers.

Distribution-shift evaluations use only 10 samples per class (~1000 images per dataset). At this scale, differences of a few percentage points are within noise, and conclusions about robustness (or its absence) are not statistically supported.

The individual techniques have limited novelty: likelihood smoothing is essentially test-time augmentation with noise on VQ features; partial-scale candidate pruning is a standard coarse-to-fine two-stage procedure instantiated on VAR's multi-scale structure; CCA finetuning is adopted wholesale from Chen et al. (2024b). The combination is useful engineering but not a substantive methodological advance.

The visual explainability contribution (token-wise PMI, Eq. 12) is a direct translation of a well-known NLP concept to autoregressive image tokens, and its evaluation is entirely qualitative (heatmaps in Figs. 3, 5-7). No quantitative faithfulness metrics (e.g., deletion/insertion, pointing game) or comparisons against established saliency methods (Grad-CAM, etc.) are provided, so the claim that this offers genuinely better explainability is unsupported.

The catastrophic forgetting experiment is a very small proof of concept: 10 classes of ImageNet, 2 tasks, one VAR-d8, one ResNet-50. VARC+ achieves lower Task-1 accuracy (72.4) than even the CWR baseline (83.2), so the evidence for 'inherent resistance to forgetting' is thin, and the conclusion about merging classifiers across datasets is speculative.

The overall practical significance remains questionable: even with the 160× speed-up, inference takes ~31 minutes per evaluation set versus seconds for discriminative models, and the method inherits all the standard weaknesses of generative classifiers. The paper acknowledges generative classifiers 'remain an underexplored direction,' which is an accurate but unconvincing justification for acceptance.

Several important experimental details are underspecified in the main text, e.g., the variance σ² and sample count S for smoothing are only partially justified, and the sensitivity of the three-stage pruning pipeline to its hyperparameters (K = (10, 3, 1)) is not ablated.

strengths: The paper introduces a new, sensible direction: using visual autoregressive (VAR) models as generative classifiers, exploiting their tractable likelihood — a genuinely underexplored alternative to the diffusion-centric literature, with preliminary prior work limited to Jaini et al. (2023).

The efficiency result is concrete and significant: A-VARC+ achieves accuracy within ~1% of the diffusion classifier on ImageNet-100 while delivering a 160× speed-up (31 min vs. 83 hours), which meaningfully improves the practical applicability of generative classifiers.

The comparative analysis is well-controlled and honest: restricting to class-conditional models trained on ImageNet to isolate the effect of the generative objective, and candidly reporting that the robustness properties of diffusion classifiers do NOT transfer to VAR is a valuable, honest negative finding that clarifies the source of diffusion-specific robustness.

The two proposed techniques (likelihood smoothing to address token-map sensitivity, and partial-scale candidate pruning exploiting coarse-to-fine structure) are well-motivated, and the ablation (Table 2) cleanly separates their individual contributions.

The token-wise pointwise mutual information framework for visual and contrastive explainability is a natural and appealing extension enabled by the tractable token likelihood, with qualitative analysis including failure cases.
The class-incremental learning proof-of-concept connects back to prior generative-classifier work (Van De Ven et al., 2021) and demonstrates a practical advantage over discriminative baselines.

The appendix analysis of the generative-vs-discriminative trade-off across VAR model sizes (Table 4, Fig. 4) provides an interesting insight (class-condition dilution in larger models) and suggests future research directions.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed evaluation subset listings (WordNet IDs), pseudo-code, and pointers to public pretrained models and code.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the individual components: likelihood smoothing is essentially ensembling over tokenization noise, candidate pruning follows the established two-stage strategy of Li et al. (2023), and CCA is borrowed directly from Chen et al. (2024b). The contribution is primarily the combination/adaptation of existing pieces to VAR rather than fundamentally new methods.

Absolute classification performance remains clearly below discriminative baselines (89.32 vs. 94.20 for ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-100), and inference time (31 min) is still orders of magnitude slower than discriminative classifiers (seconds). The claimed practical advantage is thus confined to comparisons against other generative classifiers, weakening the significance of the efficiency claim.

Evaluation scale is small: results are on ImageNet-100 (100 classes) rather than full ImageNet, and distribution-shift datasets use only 10 samples per class, which introduces substantial sampling variance; no confidence intervals, standard errors, or multiple seeds are reported.

The headline 160× speed-up compares against a very slow diffusion baseline (DC(25,250) at 83 hours); a fairer efficiency framing against stronger/faster generative classifiers or sampling-based diffusion variants would strengthen the claim.

It is unclear on which data CCA finetuning is performed (full ImageNet vs. the ImageNet-100 subset used for evaluation); if finetuning data overlaps with the evaluation distribution, the gains could be partially attributed to distribution-specific adaptation.

The class-incremental learning experiment is a very small proof-of-concept (10 classes, 2 tasks) with no comparison to modern continual learning methods beyond CWR, limiting the strength of the 'inherent resistance to catastrophic forgetting' claim.

The robustness section largely reports negative results (VAR does not inherit diffusion robustness), which is informative but reduces the positive contribution of this analysis; no attempt is made to explain mechanistically why the generative objective alone does not confer robustness.

No comparison against other autoregressive backbones (e.g., LlamaGen-style raster-scan AR models or PixelCNN-style models as classifiers), which would help verify that the claimed advantages are specific to VAR's next-scale prediction rather than AR likelihoods in general.
Runtime comparisons are conducted across heterogeneous hardware with estimates for the diffusion classifier, introducing uncertainty into the speed-up numbers.
No commitment to releasing the authors' own code/implementation, only links to third-party pretrained models, which limits reproducibility of the full pipeline.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: generative classifiers are computationally bottlenecked by diffusion-based ELBO estimation, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that VAR's tractable likelihood yields a large efficiency win (89x fewer GFLOPs than the 2-stage diffusion classifier at comparable ImageNet-100 accuracy).

Well-designed inference pipeline: the three-stage A-VARC design (partial-scale coarse pruning -> full-scale filtering -> smoothed likelihood) is sensible and empirically validated; Figure 2 and the token-count analysis (first 5 scales = ~8% of tokens) give a clear rationale for partial-scale pruning.

Comprehensive and honest comparative evaluation across multiple model families (ResNet, ViT, IBINN, MeanFlow, DiT-based diffusion) and five distribution-shift datasets, with an unusually candid analysis: the paper explicitly reports that diffusion-style distribution-shift robustness does NOT transfer to VAR and provides a plausible hypothesis (denoising training paradigm rather than the generative objective).

Valuable additional analyses beyond raw accuracy: quantitative evaluation of token-wise mutual information as an attribution method using insertion/deletion AUC against LIME/SHAP baselines, a model-size study revealing a generative-vs-discriminative trade-off (Table 7/Fig. 10), and a proof-of-concept class-incremental learning experiment showing no catastrophic forgetting.

Thorough ablations (number of smoothing samples S, smoothing variance sigma, combination with pruning, per-component contributions in Table 2), detailed implementation/reproducibility information, code release, and an explicit LLM-use statement.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core observation (tractable AR likelihood -> cheap classification) is fairly direct; likelihood smoothing is essentially test-time augmentation with feature-space Gaussian noise, candidate pruning is a standard cascaded two-stage scheme, and the accuracy gains largely come from applying the existing CCA finetuning objective (Chen et al., 2024b) to VAR rather than a new method.

Scope of empirical claims is narrow: all main results are on ImageNet-100 (a 100-class subset), not the full 1,000-class ImageNet that the efficiency argument most concerns; the linear-in-classes cost issue, a central motivation, is only mitigated in a 100-class setting and never demonstrated at scale.

Absolute performance remains well below discriminative baselines on ImageNet and most shift datasets (e.g., 89.32 vs 94.20 for ViT-B/16 on ImageNet), and generative classifiers are still ~80-800x more expensive in GFLOPs than discriminative models, weakening the practical significance of the efficiency claim.

Robustness evaluation is based on only 10 samples per class on shift datasets, which introduces substantial sampling noise for small accuracy differences (e.g., A-VARC+ vs DC differences within a few points); no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

The class-incremental learning experiment is a very small proof of concept (10 classes, 2 tasks), so the claim that VAR-based classifiers 'naturally adapt' to CIL is under-supported relative to how prominently it is featured.

Some claims rest on weak evidence: the explanation for why MeanFlow underperforms DiT, and the hypothesis for why classifier-free guidance hurts likelihood-based classification, are plausible but speculative and untested.

strengths: First systematic study of VAR (visual autoregressive) models as generative classifiers; the tractable likelihood enables single-forward-pass classification, a genuine and timely alternative to costly diffusion-based classifiers.
Strong efficiency result: A-VARC+ matches the two-stage DiT-based diffusion classifier on ImageNet-100 within ~1% accuracy while requiring ~89x less computation (4,649 vs 28,210 GFLOPs).

Comprehensive comparative evaluation across discriminative (ResNets, ViTs) and generative (IBINN, diffusion, rectified-flow) baselines, with multiple distribution-shift benchmarks and a clear efficiency metric (GFLOPs).

Reasonably thorough ablations: smoothing sample count (S), smoothing variance (sigma), partial-scale pruning, model-size trade-off between generative (FID) and discriminative performance, plus honest analysis of failure cases.

The paper is candid about negative findings, e.g., VAR classifiers do not inherit the OOD robustness of diffusion-based methods, and discriminative models still dominate overall; the appendix analysis of the generative/discriminative trade-off is informative.

Additional analyses (token-wise mutual information explainability with insertion/deletion metrics, and a class-incremental learning proof-of-concept) go beyond accuracy and explore properties unique to likelihood-based classifiers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The three components are largely standard engineering: likelihood smoothing is Monte Carlo averaging over input perturbations (closely related to randomized smoothing/test-time augmentation), partial-scale candidate pruning is a conventional coarse-to-fine cascade adapted to VAR scales, and CCA is borrowed wholesale from Chen et al. (2024b) with no modification.

Narrow evaluation scope. All main experiments use ImageNet-100 (not full ImageNet-1k); distribution-shift evaluations use only 10 samples per class (~1,000 images per dataset), making accuracy estimates on IN-V2, IN-R, IN-Sketch, ObjectNet, and IN-A statistically fragile.

Generative classifiers remain far behind discriminative models: A-VARC+ (89.32) trails ViT-B/16 (93.22) on ImageNet-100, and even the 'efficient' method needs ~4,600 GFLOPs vs. 1.3-59 GFLOPs for discriminative models. The practical significance of the claimed efficiency gain is therefore questionable.

The headline robustness story of generative classifiers largely does not transfer to VAR (no advantage on IN-V2/R/Sketch/ObjectNet), weakening the paper's motivating narrative; explainability and CIL results are mostly qualitative or tiny-scale (10 classes, 2 tasks).
No comparison against CLIP-style zero-shot or multimodal classifiers, which are the natural strong baselines for robust/efficient classification in this regime.

Costs of CCA finetuning (compute, data, and its effect on the generative quality of the underlying VAR model) are not reported in the main text, and hyperparameters like the smoothing sigma appear only in the appendix.

The title and framing ('Secretly an Efficient and Explainable Generative Classifier') oversell what is a careful but incremental application study; the CIL and explainability claims are proof-of-concept rather than established advantages.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated direction: adapting the recent VAR backbone (Tian et al., 2024) to generative classification, exploiting its tractable likelihood to avoid the massive Monte Carlo overhead of ELBO-based diffusion classifiers.

The proposed A-VARC pipeline (likelihood smoothing, partial-scale candidate pruning, CCA finetuning) is well engineered, and the headline result is convincing: comparable accuracy to the 2-stage DiT diffusion classifier on ImageNet-100 with 89x less compute.

Comprehensive and fairly conducted comparative study across discriminative (ResNet, ViT) and generative (IBINN, diffusion, rectified-flow) baselines on ImageNet-100 and five distribution-shift datasets, with matched sample budgets for DC baselines.

Honest and insightful negative findings: VAR classifiers do not inherit the distribution-shift robustness of diffusion models, and larger VAR models degrade in discriminative ability (Appendix D trade-off analysis) — this adds understanding rather than just claiming wins.

Two genuinely interesting extensions: token-wise mutual information (TMI) for visual explainability with quantitative insertion/deletion evaluation against LIME/SHAP, and a proof-of-concept class-incremental learning result without replay data.
Strong reproducibility: code release, pseudo-code, detailed subsets (WordNet IDs), hyperparameter and ablation details (S, sigma, number of scales).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the individual components: likelihood smoothing is a straightforward Monte Carlo perturbation in latent space, and partial-scale pruning is a fairly standard cascade/two-stage filtering idea adapted to the multi-scale VAR structure. The main contribution is the combination and system-level insight rather than a new technique.

Evaluation is confined to ImageNet-100 (100 classes, 50 samples/class); the central scalability claim (cost scaling linearly with number of classes) is never demonstrated on full ImageNet-1k, which is precisely where the efficiency argument matters most.

Even with A-VARC+, the generative classifier remains below discriminative models (89.32 vs 94.20 top-1 for ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-100) and is still orders of magnitude more expensive in GFLOPs (4649 vs 16.9), so the practical significance of the achieved operating point is debatable.

The class-incremental learning experiment is a very small proof-of-concept (10 classes, two 5-class tasks) with training-from-scratch discriminative baselines; it does not establish the claim at a meaningful scale.

The absence of diffusion-like robustness to distribution shifts for the VAR classifier weakens one of the main advertised advantages of generative classifiers, leaving the paper's value proposition somewhat narrower than the framing suggests.
Ablations show smoothing saturates quickly and CCA slightly hurts some shift benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet-A), so accuracy gains come with trade-offs that are discussed but not fully resolved.

Some presentation issues: heavy reliance on the appendix for key implementation details (three-stage procedure, sigma value), and Fig. 1's noise-perturbation motivation is anecdotal rather than quantitatively tied to the smoothing gain.
